reference.source: OMIM / GeneReviews (NCBI) and inherited bone-marrow-failure consensus guidance
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive inherited bone-marrow-failure and ribosomopathy syndrome, most often caused by biallelic variants in SBDS
Classic combination is exocrine pancreatic insufficiency with malabsorption and steatorrhoea plus bone marrow dysfunction
Neutropenia is the most common and characteristic cytopenia, often intermittent, and predisposes to recurrent infection
Skeletal abnormalities include metaphyseal dysplasia, short stature and thoracic dystrophy
Pancreatic dysfunction may improve with age, and serum trypsinogen and isoamylase are useful biochemical markers
There is a significant risk of progression to aplastic anaemia, myelodysplastic syndrome and acute myeloid leukaemia
The SBDS protein participates in ribosome maturation, placing the disorder among the ribosomopathies

Management centres on pancreatic enzyme and fat-soluble vitamin replacement, infection control, and marrow surveillance, with haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for marrow failure or malignant transformation
reference.pathophysiology: Shwachman-Diamond syndrome most commonly results from biallelic variants in SBDS, whose product cooperates in the maturation of the large ribosomal subunit and release of the anti-association factor eIF6. Defective ribosome assembly impairs protein translation in highly proliferative tissues, producing pancreatic acinar hypoplasia with fatty replacement, ineffective and reduced haematopoiesis, and skeletal dysplasia. Genomic instability of the marrow underlies the predisposition to clonal evolution and leukaemic transformation.
additionalDifferentials: Other inherited bone-marrow-failure syndromes such as Fanconi anaemia and dyskeratosis congenita
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count over time to document neutropenia and other cytopenias
Faecal elastase and serum trypsinogen and isoamylase for pancreatic exocrine function
Molecular genetic testing of SBDS and related genes
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine with cytogenetics for dysplasia and clonal change
Fat-soluble vitamin levels and nutritional assessment
redFlags: New or worsening cytopenias suggesting progression to aplastic anaemia or myelodysplasia
Cytogenetic clonal abnormality or blasts indicating leukaemic transformation
Severe or recurrent infection during neutropenia
Failure to thrive from uncontrolled malabsorption
reference.prognosis: With enzyme replacement and infection management many patients do well in childhood, but the lifelong risk of marrow failure, myelodysplasia and acute myeloid leukaemia dominates long-term prognosis and mandates surveillance; haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is used for marrow failure or malignant transformation.
pitfalls: Attributing the malabsorption to cystic fibrosis without genetic and biochemical confirmation
Being falsely reassured when pancreatic function improves with age while marrow risk persists
Missing intermittent neutropenia on a single normal blood count
Neglecting regular marrow and cytogenetic surveillance for clonal evolution
